What to have ready for when the locksmith arrives: something that shows they belong at that address, since the Table E lockout authority row has the trade asking (a licence with the address, other identification, a neighbour who can vouch; a business sends an authority letter). What to do meanwhile: leave the key and the door alone rather than force either, and keep clear of broken glass after a break in. Never a word on how the door will be opened. faq_slots.question: Why will my uPVC door only lock if I lift the handle hard?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Use the assigned symptom's meaning and its linked local issue. Then what the local housing adds (the age of the estate's doors, from the dossier), then the fix: hinges and keeps adjusted first, the gearbox replaced only where it has failed, never a new cylinder as the cure (Table B done badly). faq_slots.question: Do I need a whole new lock, or just a new cylinder?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Honest first: on most uPVC and composite doors, and many timber ones, the part the key goes into comes out on its own (Table A lock fitting materials), so after a move, a loss or years of wear the smaller job is swapping that part and cutting fresh keys (Table F: like for like hardware in sound existing preparations costs less). Then when the whole lock is the job: a lock body or gearbox that has failed, a timber door with no lock to the standard the policy asks for, a door being brought up to what an insurer or an escape route needs (Table A British Standard stages; Table E door insurance). A cylinder that resists being forced where the Table E snapping row applies, said as what it resists and never how the attack works. Never a standard's number, never a brand.

This business's own membership, vetting or checks only from the client values (the accreditation fields), named as they are recorded there and never implied; where nothing is recorded, close on how the customer can check who is at the door: the name on the van and the invoice matching the business they rang, and a price agreed before the visit only where the price_agreed_before_work practice is confirmed. cards.title: Your insurer has asked what locks are on the doors
cards.brief: A situation card, not a fault: a renewal form that asks about the locks, a new policy with a security condition, a claim turned down somewhere else that the customer has heard about. The one cause this card makes: a condition in the policy wording, not anything wrong with the door. cards.title: Moved in, and not sure who still has a key
cards.brief: A situation card: a completion day, a new tenancy, a lodger gone, a set of keys lost on a night out with nothing to say whose they were. The one cause this card makes: keys cut for the lock over the years that were never handed back, and still turn it. Say what the work usually involves in plain words from the Table A lock fitting and lock repairs rows: on a uPVC, composite or many a timber door the cylinder comes out and a new one goes in with new keys, so the old keys turn nothing; a whole new lock only where the lock body itself is worn or the policy wants a different kind (card 1 owns that). Say who the customer is, never a scare: nothing about burglars or risk. A landlord's change between tenancies reads as after a tenant has left, never as a way to keep one out while they still live there (Table E landlord lock changes; a tenant's change does not shut out another lawful occupier either: Table E tenant lock changes). Never how a key or a lock is defeated. On a Security System Supplier page the card reads as codes or fobs handed out over the years on a door entry system and never cancelled.

cards.title: A lock that's getting harder to use
cards.brief: Problem led, the early warning across the trade: a handle that needs more force each month, a key that has to be wiggled, a door that has to be lifted or pulled before it will lock, a latch that no longer catches (Table B lock repairs and uPVC rows, in the customer's words). The one cause this card makes: wear in the mechanism that shows as stiffness long before it fails. Why it matters without alarm, from the Table B skipped rows: the strain keeps loading the mechanism until it will not lock, or will not open, and that tends to happen with the door shut; a repair while it is only stiff is the smaller job. What the fix usually involves from Table A lock repairs: the cylinder, the lock body, the keep and the alignment looked at together, the worn part adjusted or replaced, the door tested from both sides; never a new cylinder alone as the cure for a worn gearbox (Table B done badly). Link the lock repairs or uPVC repairs page where LINKABLE PAGES has one. Not the dropped door, not the worn gearbox, not the worn key by name: the service pages own those causes. On a Security System Supplier page the card reads as a door release or a reader that works some days and not others, from the wiring or the door's alignment; otherwise as the Locksmith's.
cards.mechanism: wear in the mechanism that shows as stiffness long before it fails
needs: uPVC door and window lock repairs

cards.title: Keys for a let, a shop or a block
cards.brief: A situation card for the landlord and business reader (the pack's third reader): a let changing hands, a shop with staff who come and go, a block with one shared door and many flats, an office where nobody is sure how many keys are out. The one cause this card makes: too many keys in circulation and no record of who holds which (Table B master key systems: a missing master key, copies nobody can account for). What the work gives them, from the Table A master key and key cutting rows: the doors mapped and who needs to get through which, cylinders keyed to that plan, keys issued against a record, and where it suits a restricted key that is only cut through an authorised route with the card (Table E restricted keys: system specific, never a ban on copying every key). On a shared or commercial door the escape side comes first: an exit door has to open easily from inside, as the Table C fire safety and HMO rows state it, said in plain words and never with an Act's name. Records that name people bring duties for whoever runs the system (Table C data protection), said in one plain line. Never fear, never 'control who gets in' as a pitch: keys and access, plainly. On a Security System Supplier page the card reads as fobs and codes in place of keys, with the same record and the same escape rule.

cards.title: Locked out, with the keys on the wrong side
cards.brief: The door swung shut on the latch with the keys on the table, keys lost on the way home, a phone running down on a doorstep after dark (Table B lockouts, in the customer's words). The one cause this card makes: a door that locked behind them and nothing in their hand to open it. Why it cannot wait: nobody is getting in, and a lock left jammed stays jammed (Table B skipped). What the customer does first: ring from where they are, have something that shows they belong at the address ready for when the locksmith arrives (Table E lockout authority: a licence with the address, other identification, a neighbour who can vouch), and leave the door alone rather than force it. What usually happens when they call, from the Table A lockouts stages: the right to enter checked, the lock and the door looked at, the way in that leaves the least mark chosen where the lock allows it, drilling only as the last option and a replacement lock after it, anything that failed found and the door tested before the locksmith leaves. Written as how the trade works, never as this business's promise that the door comes to no harm (Table E entry damage). Nothing on how entry is made. cards.title: A key that's snapped, or a lock that won't turn
cards.brief: Half a key in the hand and half in the door, a key that turns and turns with the door staying shut, a uPVC handle that will not lift with the door closed (Table B emergency and lockouts rows: 'the key has snapped', 'the key turns but the door stays shut', 'the handle moves but nothing opens'). The one cause this card makes: a broken key or a mechanism that has failed in the locked position, so the door is stuck whichever way it is tried. Why it cannot wait: the door will not open or will not lock, and forcing it adds damage to the repair (Table B done badly). What the customer does first: stop turning or pulling at it, keep the broken piece if it came out, and say on the phone what kind of door and lock it is. What usually happens when they call, from the Table A emergency stages: the fault identified, the door opened, the failed part (a cylinder, a gearbox, a lock body) repaired or replaced if authorised, the lock tested and the keys handed over; entry alone is not the job, since a mechanism that has failed once fails again (Table B lockouts skipped). Never promise a part on the van for an obsolete mechanism (Table F). Nothing on how the key is removed or the door opened. On the Security System Supplier page the card reads as a door release that has failed shut.
cards.mechanism: a broken key or a mechanism failed in the locked position

cards.title: A door that won't shut after a break in
cards.brief: Glass gone from a panel, a lock forced, a frame split at the keep, a door that no longer closes, a hole where a lock was (Table B burglary repairs, in the customer's words). The one cause this card makes: a forced lock or a split frame with nothing left to hold the door shut. Why it cannot wait: an opening that will not close cannot be secured until it is boarded or repaired (Table B skipped). What the customer does first, from the Table E after a burglary row: the police report and the insurance claim are theirs to make, and the insurer will want the emergency repairs recorded and the receipts kept; keep clear of broken glass; the locksmith's part is making the opening secure and recording what was done, not the investigation and not the claim decision. What usually happens when they call, from the Table A stages: the opening checked as safe, the broken glass or gap boarded for now, the door and frame repaired where that can be done, the forced locks replaced, the work tested and written up; a cylinder alone where the frame is split leaves the door weak (Table B done badly), so the permanent repair may be a return visit (Table F). Never a crime figure, never 'they will be back', never the neighbourhood as unsafe. Whether the business deals with the insurer only from the client values.
cards.mechanism: a forced lock or a split frame with nothing left to hold the door

cards.title: Keys gone missing that still fit the door

Why it is a same day matter rather than a someday one, said once and plainly without fear: for as long as the old key fits, the lock is not doing its job. What the customer does first: nothing to the door; ring and say which doors the keys opened. From the Table A lock fitting and lock repairs rows: the cylinder is swapped and fresh keys cut, which leaves the missing set useless. A complete replacement only where the body is worn or the policy wants a different kind (Table F: like for like in the existing cut out is the smaller job). A landlord's change only after the tenant has lawfully left (Table E landlord lock changes), never as a way to shut one out. Never burglary statistics, never a neighbourhood described as a target. On a Security System Supplier page the card reads as a lost fob cancelled on the system.

cards.title: The door only locks if you lift or pull it
cards.brief: Problem led: the handle has to be heaved up, the door pulled towards you or lifted before the key will turn, and it locks easily with the door open (Table B uPVC: 'I have to pull the door to lock it', 'it locks when open but not when shut'). The one cause this card makes: a door that has dropped on its hinges, so the locking points miss their keeps. Say why it matters without alarm, from the Table B skipped row: every forced lock loads the mechanism a little more until it fails. What the fix usually involves from Table A uPVC repairs: the door checked open and closed, the hinges and keeps adjusted, every locking point checked, and only then any part replaced; a new cylinder cures nothing here (Table B done badly). Leads on uPVC door and window lock repairs and Lock repairs. On an urgent page when the emergency layout is off (the client has not confirmed call outs) the card reads as the door that will one day refuse to open, from the Table B row for that page. On the Auto locksmith page the card reads as a key that opens the door but will not start the car (Table B auto): the cut blade is not the whole key.

cards.title: The handle won't lift, even with the door open
cards.brief: Problem led: the handle flops or jams, nothing happens when it is lifted, and it does the same with the door wide open (Table B uPVC: 'the handle won't lift'; Table E uPVC faults: a door that will not lock even open points at the gearbox). The one cause this card makes: the gearbox in the door edge has worn out. Why it matters, from the Table B skipped row: a failed gearbox can stop the door locking or opening, and it tends to go with the door shut. What the fix usually involves from Table A: the gearbox or the full mechanism replaced, the hinges and keeps checked at the same time so the new one is not loaded as the old one was (Table B done badly: adjusting only the keep leaves a failed gearbox); an obsolete mechanism may have to be sourced (Table F), said without a promise of a part on the day. Leads on uPVC door and window lock repairs. Never how the door is opened when it has already failed shut: the emergency pages own that.
cards.mechanism: a gearbox worn out in the edge of the door
needs: uPVC door and window lock repairs

cards.title: A key that's getting harder to turn
cards.brief: Problem led: a key that has to be jiggled, one that goes in but will not turn without a push, a spare that sticks where the original does not (Table B lock repairs: 'the key is hard to turn'; lock fitting: 'the key sticks'; key cutting: 'the spare sticks', 'a copied key won't turn'). The one cause this card makes: a worn key, or a cylinder worn to match it. Say what that means plainly: a key cut from a worn original carries the wear into the copy (Table B key cutting done badly), so a spare that sticks is often the original's fault, not the cutting. What the fix usually involves from Table A lock repairs and key cutting: the cylinder, the lock body and the alignment looked at, the worn cylinder replaced with new keys, or a key cut to code rather than copied from the worn one. Leads on Lock repairs and Key cutting; on the Auto locksmith page the card reads as a worn or broken blade (Table B auto). Never how a lock is picked or got past; never a brand.
cards.mechanism: a worn key, or a cylinder worn to match it

cards.title: A door that sticks when the weather warms up
cards.brief: Problem led, the one weather fact in this trade: a door that locked fine all winter and binds on the first warm week, a latch that no longer catches, a handle that has worked loose (Table B uPVC: 'the door sticks in hot weather'; Table B lock repairs: 'the latch doesn't catch', 'the handle is loose'; Table A uPVC timing: warm weather exposes alignment faults). The one cause this card makes: a door swollen tight in warm weather, pressing the mechanism against its keeps. Say first that a tight door in a heatwave is common and does not mean the lock has failed (Table E hot weather: the wrong version is that summer heat proves the cylinder has gone). What the fix usually involves from Table A: the hinges and keeps checked and adjusted as well as the mechanism, the loose handle refixed, the latch lined up with its keep. Leads on uPVC door and window lock repairs and Lock repairs. Not the dropped door (card 1) and not the gearbox (card 2).

cards.brief: The customer's situation: a renewal form that asks what locks are on the doors and windows, a new policy with a security condition, a mortgage lender or a letting agent asking the same. What decides it, from the Table E door and window insurance rows: the conditions in that insurer's own wording, which tend to specify the sort of lock an outside door carries and, with some policies, a lock on each opening window downstairs; whether the door is a timber door that takes a lock to that standard or a uPVC or composite door whose cylinder and handle are what the condition turns on (Table E snapping and TS rows, said as what the cylinder resists and never how); whether the door or window is an escape route, which decides keyless exit (Table A British Standard and window locks stages; Table C escape rows, with 'usually'). cards.brief: The customer's situation: a holiday let with guests every week, a carer or a cleaner who needs to get in while they are out, a family that keeps losing keys, a shop or an office with staff who change, a block or a site with doors that different people may and may not open. cards.title: Getting back in without wrecking the door
cards.brief: The locked out customer's first fear, written as how good work goes rather than as a promise: a door that swung shut on its latch is a different problem from one somebody locked with a key, and which of the two it is decides how the locksmith goes about it and whether anything is left to show for it (Table A lockouts: identify the lock and the door's condition, assess entry without damage, drilling as the last resort followed by a replacement lock). The one cause this card makes: which lock is actually holding the door, the latch or the deadlock. What usually happens when they call: the right to enter checked (Table E lockout authority), the door looked at, the way in that leaves the least mark tried first where the lock allows it, and where a lock has to be drilled a new one fitted before the locksmith leaves. Some locks cannot be opened any other way, so no promise is made (Table E entry damage); 'without damage' as this business's practice only from the client values. cards.title: A lock that has failed with the door shut
cards.brief: The handle moves and nothing opens, the key turns and the door stays locked, a uPVC handle that will not lift with the door closed (Table B lockouts: 'the lock is jammed', 'the handle moves but nothing opens'; Table E uPVC faults: gearbox failure can prevent locking or opening). The one cause this card makes: a failed gearbox or lock body, so the door stays shut whatever the key does. Why it cannot wait: the door is out of use, and forcing it adds a frame repair to a lock repair. What usually happens when they call, from the Table A emergency stages: the door opened, the failed part identified and replaced if authorised, the lock tested from both sides, the keys handed over; getting in alone is not the job, since a mechanism that has failed once fails again (Table B lockouts skipped). An obsolete mechanism may need a part ordered, so the door is left secure in the meantime and a date agreed (Table F); never promise a part on the van. Leads on Emergency locksmith; Lockouts and gaining entry reads it the same. Nothing on how the door is opened.
cards.mechanism: a failed gearbox or lock body, so the door stays shut whatever the key does

cards.title: Boarded tonight, repaired properly after
cards.brief: Glass gone from a door or window, a frame split where the lock was forced, a door that will not close (Table B burglary repairs, in the customer's words). The one cause this card makes: an opening that cannot be secured until the glass, the frame or the lock is replaced. What usually happens when they call, from the Table A burglary stages: the opening checked as safe to work on, the gap or the glass boarded, the door and frame repaired where that can be done tonight, the forced locks replaced, the work tested and written up; where the frame or a whole door has to be replaced the boarding holds until the return visit (Table F: temporary security plus a permanent return visit). What the insurer will want, from the Table E after a burglary row: the emergency repairs recorded and the receipts kept; the locksmith secures and documents, the insurer decides the claim and the police the investigation, never the other way round. A cylinder alone with a split frame leaves the door weak (Table B done badly). Leads on Burglary repairs and boarding up. Never a crime figure, never the street as a target, never 'they come back'. Whether the business deals with the insurer only from the client values.
cards.mechanism: an opening that can't be secured until the glass, frame or lock is replaced

cards.title: Proving it's your door
cards.brief: The honest card about the one question every locksmith asks on a doorstep at night. The one cause this card makes: a door is opened only for someone with the right to be behind it. From the Table E lockout authority row, said as the trade's own practice and never as a law: a licence with the address on it, other identification, a neighbour who can confirm who they are, or an officer present; a business sends a letter or an order; for a car the keeper's document is one part of the check, not proof on its own (Table E V5C).
